passages.t: Sons at Hebron, and Abner's quarrel with his king
passages.happening:
The war between the two houses drags on. ‘And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker’ (verse 1).

Six sons are born to David at Hebron, each by a different mother: Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel; Chileab, by Abigail; Absalom, the son of Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; Adonijah, the son of Haggith; Shephatiah; and Ithream (verses 2-5).

In the north, Abner has been making himself strong in the house of Saul. Then Ish-bosheth accuses him: “Why did you sleep with my father’s concubine?” (verse 7). The woman is Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. Abner is furious. He has been loyal to Saul's house, he says, and now he is accused over a woman. He swears to do for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to bring the kingdom over to David's throne ‘from Dan to Beersheba’ (verse 10). Ish-bosheth is too afraid of Abner to say another word (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
These are David's seven and a half years at Hebron, roughly 1010 to 1003 BC. The list of sons is the list of a rising king's marriages. Most of his wives come from Judah and its region, but Maacah is a king's daughter from Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee. A marriage like that was a treaty as well as a wedding, and it placed an ally on the northern flank of Ish-bosheth's land. A first reader would mark three names. Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah will fill the tragedies of David's later years, and Absalom will one day flee to his grandfather in Geshur (13:37).

A king's concubines were part of his household, and in that world they were a public sign of his authority. To take a dead king's concubine could be read as a claim to his throne. That is why Ish-bosheth's question is so serious, and why Abner answers so hotly. The narrator never says whether Abner had in fact slept with Rizpah.

Abner was the real power in the north, and the weak king could not stand against him. ‘From Dan to Beersheba’ became the standard way of naming the whole land, from its northern edge to its southern one.
passages.later:
The same move is made again in Solomon's day. When David's son Adonijah asked to marry Abishag, the young woman who had cared for David in his old age, Solomon heard it as a claim to the throne: ‘you might as well request the kingdom for him’ (1 Kings 2:22).

The phrase for the whole land was already old. When the tribes gathered against Gibeah, ‘all the Israelites from Dan to Beersheba’ came out (Judges 20:1).
passages.asks: Abner served Saul's house for years and turned in a single afternoon over a wounded pride. Ask what would move your own loyalty, and whether it rests on anything deeper than being treated well.

passages.t: A covenant offered, and Michal taken from Paltiel
passages.happening:
Abner sends messengers to David: “To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and surely my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you” (verse 12). David agrees, on one condition. Abner must bring Michal, Saul's daughter, David's first wife.

David sends to Ish-bosheth: “Give me back my wife, Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred Philistine foreskins” (verse 14). So Ish-bosheth takes Michal from her husband, Paltiel. ‘Her husband followed her, weeping all the way to Bahurim’ (verse 16), until Abner tells him to go back, and he goes home.

Abner speaks to the elders of Israel. They had wanted David as king before, he says, and the LORD has promised to save Israel from the Philistines through his servant David (verses 17-18). He wins over the Benjamites too, and then comes to Hebron with twenty men. David holds a feast for them. Abner promises to gather all Israel to make a covenant with the king, ‘So David dismissed Abner, and he went in peace’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
A covenant was a sworn agreement, binding both sides, and it was often sealed with a meal, like the feast David gives Abner here. Kingship in Israel was meant to rest on covenant, a relationship with duties on both sides before the LORD.

David's demand for Michal is both personal and political. She was his first wife, won at great cost (1 Samuel 18:25-27), and then given by Saul to another man while David was a fugitive. Taking her back renewed David's tie to Saul's family and strengthened his claim to Saul's kingdom.

The cost falls on others. Michal is moved between men as a piece in their politics, and the text gives her no word at all. Paltiel follows her, weeping, as far as Bahurim. It is one of the saddest scenes in the book, and the narrator lets it stand without comment.

Abner's words to the elders frame David's kingship as God's way of saving his people. The verb to save is yasha, the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. Whether Abner is quoting a word of the LORD not recorded elsewhere, or summing up earlier promises, the chapter does not say.
passages.later: The psalms remember David as the LORD's chosen servant in the same words: ‘I have found My servant David; with My sacred oil I have anointed him’ (Psalm 89:20).
passages.asks: Paltiel's tears are the only feelings the chapter records in this exchange. Ask who pays for the agreements powerful people make, and whether anyone notices them. And ask whose quiet grief around you has gone unseen.

passages.t: Joab murders Abner, and David mourns
passages.happening:
Just after Abner leaves, Joab comes back from a raid. He hears that Abner has been to the king and gone away in peace, and he confronts David: “What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why did you dismiss him? Now he is getting away!” (verse 24). Abner came only to deceive him, Joab says.

Then, without David's knowledge, Joab sends messengers to bring Abner back. ‘When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab pulled him aside into the gateway, as if to speak to him privately’ (verse 27), and there he kills him. ‘So Abner died on account of the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel’ (verse 27).

When David hears, he declares, “I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner” (verse 28), and he calls down a curse on Joab's house. He orders Joab and all the people to tear their clothes and mourn, and he himself walks behind the bier. At the tomb he weeps aloud and sings a short lament: “Should Abner die the death of a fool?” (verse 33). He refuses food until sunset. ‘All the people took note and were pleased’ (verse 36), and all Israel is convinced that the king had no part in the murder.

Then David says to his servants, “Do you not realize that a great prince has fallen today in Israel? And I am weak this day, though anointed as king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!” (verses 38-39).
passages.hearers:
The narrator says three times that David sent Abner away in peace (verses 21, 22 and 23), so that no reader can miss David's innocence. He adds a note of his own to make the motive plain: Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel at Gibeon (verse 30).

The gateway was the town's public place, where courts sat and business was done. To kill there was to do violence in the very place of justice. And Hebron was one of the cities of refuge, set apart as places where someone who had killed could be protected until judged. Some readers see a bitter irony in Joab killing Abner in its gate, especially since Asahel had died in battle, not by murder.

David's lament asks whether Abner should die like a fool, a man caught unarmed and unbound by treachery. Torn clothes, sackcloth, walking behind the bier and fasting were the public language of grief, and David uses every one of them so that Israel will see where he stands. He calls his enemy's commander a great prince.

The chapter opened with David growing stronger. It closes with David saying he is weak. The sons of Zeruiah, his nephews, are loyal to him and fierce beyond his control, and that tension will run to the end of his life.
passages.later:
Hebron was set apart as a city of refuge in Joshua's day: ‘Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah’ (Joshua 20:7).

David did not forget. On his deathbed he told Solomon what Joab had done to Abner and to Amasa, and said, ‘do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace’ (1 Kings 2:6).
passages.hard:
Why doesn't David punish Joab for murdering Abner?

David curses Joab's house, makes him mourn in public and declares the murder evil, but he does not remove or execute him. The text gives David's own reason: though anointed, he is weak, and the sons of Zeruiah are too fierce for him. His kingdom was fragile and depended on Joab's skill in war and on the loyalty of his family, and Joab was David's nephew.

Some readers see this as political realism. Others see a failure of justice that the book records on purpose, since Joab will kill again (Amasa, in chapter 20) and act against David's wishes (Absalom, in chapter 18). That David told Solomon to deal with Joab shows he never forgot the unpunished blood. The narrator neither excuses David nor condemns him outright. He lets the consequences speak.
passages.asks: Joab's revenge grew from real grief for his brother. Ask how a real wrong done to you could turn into something that wrongs others. And ask where you, like David, have known what was right and felt too weak to do it.
